## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why does an agent that is waiting on a tool still occupy the accelerator?_

Every token an agent keeps in context leaves attention state in accelerator memory, and across the trajectories a serving node holds, that state outgrows the model's own weights. A chat request holds this state for a few seconds and releases it. An agent holds it across dozens of turns, forks it when it explores alternatives, and leaves it sitting idle while a test suite runs or a person approves an action. A serving system that treats each trajectory as one opaque, worst-case reservation runs out of memory with most of it unused, recomputes the same shared instructions on every turn, and starves active trajectories to keep paused ones warm. The fixes are known. Hold attention state in pages that branches can share, reuse the prefix across turns, and decide for each pause whether to keep, move, or drop the state. They pay off only when the harness cooperates, because the harness decides how long contexts grow, whether the prefix stays stable, and how long each tool is expected to run. In H·S·A terms, a long horizon turns into state the serving system must physically hold, so the cost of that state is set jointly by the engine that stores it and the harness that shapes it.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate a trajectory's KV footprint from model geometry, context length, and precision.
- Explain why unknown trajectory length, forks, and tool pauses strand memory under worst-case reservation.
- Explain how paged blocks and copy-on-write let branches share one prefix without copying it.
- Diagnose which harness decisions raise or break the prefix-cache hit rate across turns.
- Select retention, offload, or recomputation for a paused trajectory from its expected tool wait.
- Estimate how many concurrent trajectories a serving pool sustains given context length, prefix sharing, and tool-wait time.

:::

## From Context to KV State {#sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry}

Consider a coding agent at its twentieth turn. Its context holds the system prompt, the tool definitions, a slice of the repository, nineteen turns of reasoning and tool output, and the stack trace the last test run produced, about thirty-two thousand tokens in all. The agent has just asked the harness to run the integration suite, which takes three-quarters of a minute. For those forty-five seconds the model emits nothing, yet the attention state computed for all thirty-two thousand tokens stays on the accelerator, waiting for the test log. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering decided which tokens this call should see. This chapter follows those tokens into the serving system, where they become the dominant consumer of accelerator memory, and asks what that state costs to keep, share, and release.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the State axis highlighted."}

*This chapter covers the part of State that the serving system holds, attention state that can be paged, shared, moved, and rebuilt.*
:::

@Sec-vol3-foundation-model defined the key-value (KV) cache in one sentence. For every token in the context, each layer keeps the key and value vectors that later tokens attend to, so decoding does not recompute them. Its size follows from model geometry alone. A model with $L$ layers, $H_{\text{kv}}$ key-value heads of dimension $d_{\text{head}}$, and $b$ bytes per stored element keeps

$$m_{\text{token}} = 2 \cdot L \cdot H_{\text{kv}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot b$$ {#eq-mem-token}

bytes for every token, where the factor of two counts the key and the value. Scaling @eq-mem-token by context length, a trajectory of $S$ tokens holds $M_{\text{KV}} = S \cdot m_{\text{token}}$ bytes, growing linearly with every turn it keeps.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-geometry-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KV FOOTPRINT AND NODE CONCURRENCY FOR A 70B GROUPED-QUERY MODEL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry prose and notebook
# │          nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for; @fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy
# │          labels; reused by StaticReservation, PagedWaste, ForkSharing,
# │          ToolWaitBreakEven, AgentCapacity.
# │
# │ Goal: Derive bytes per token from model geometry and the number of
# │       trajectories one eight-accelerator node can hold at three context lengths.
# │ Show: 327,680 bytes/token; 2.7 / 10.7 / 42.9 GB per trajectory;
# │       526.0 GB KV pool; 195 / 48 / 12 concurrent trajectories.
# │ How: calc_kv_cache_size on registry geometry (Llama3_70B); node HBM from the
# │      DGX_H100 registry entry minus FP16 weights and a scenario runtime reserve.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory

class KvGeometry:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    _model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    n_layers = _model.layers
    n_kv_heads = _model.kv_heads
    d_head = _model.hidden_dim // _model.heads
    bytes_per_elem = 2  # 16-bit keys and values
    _node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    n_acc = _node.accelerators_per_node
    acc_capacity = _node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: activations and runtime buffers
    ctx_short, ctx_agent, ctx_long = 8_192, 32_768, 131_072

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, d_head, 1, 1, bytes_per_elem)
    kv_short = calc_kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, d_head, ctx_short, 1, bytes_per_elem)
    kv_agent = calc_kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, d_head, ctx_agent, 1, bytes_per_elem)
    kv_long = calc_kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, d_head, ctx_long, 1, bytes_per_elem)
    node_hbm = n_acc * acc_capacity
    weights = _model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    kv_pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    conc_short = int((kv_pool / kv_short).to("").magnitude)
    conc_agent = int((kv_pool / kv_agent).to("").magnitude)
    conc_long = int((kv_pool / kv_long).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(int(bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude) == 327_680, "KV bytes/token must equal 2 * 80 * 8 * 128 * 2")
    check(conc_short == 195 and conc_agent == 48 and conc_long == 12, f"Expected 195/48/12 trajectories, got {conc_short}/{conc_agent}/{conc_long}")
    check(conc_short // conc_long == 16, "Prose claims a sixteen-fold collapse from 8k to 128k")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    n_layers_str = fmt_int(n_layers)
    ctx_short_str = fmt_int(ctx_short)
    ctx_agent_str = fmt_int(ctx_agent)
    ctx_long_str = fmt_int(ctx_long)
    n_kv_heads_str = fmt_int(n_kv_heads)
    d_head_str = fmt_int(d_head)
    bytes_per_token_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude)
    mb_per_token_str = fmt_memory(bytes_per_token, unit=MB, precision=2)
    kv_short_str = fmt_memory(kv_short, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_agent_str = fmt_memory(kv_agent, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_long_str = fmt_memory(kv_long, unit=GB, precision=1)
    n_acc_str = fmt_int(n_acc)
    node_hbm_str = fmt_memory(node_hbm, unit=GB, precision=1)
    weights_str = fmt_memory(weights, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reserve_str = fmt_memory(runtime_reserve, unit=GB, precision=0)
    kv_pool_str = fmt_memory(kv_pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    conc_short_str = fmt_int(conc_short)
    conc_agent_str = fmt_int(conc_agent)
    conc_long_str = fmt_int(conc_long)
```

The formula becomes a budget once a model is fixed. Take a 70-billion-parameter model with grouped-query attention, where several query heads share each key-value head [@ainslie2023gqa]: `{python} KvGeometry.n_layers_str` layers, `{python} KvGeometry.n_kv_heads_str` key-value heads of dimension `{python} KvGeometry.d_head_str`, and 16-bit storage. @Fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy traces one agent context through that geometry, and the worked estimate below turns it into a concurrency ceiling.

::: {#fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Agent Context to KV State**: A 32,768-token agent context (system prompt, tool definitions, workspace, turn history, and the latest observation) becomes key and value tensors for every layer. The per-token footprint of the 70B grouped-query model sets how many such trajectories fit in one node's KV pool." fig-alt="Top panel shows an agent context split into system prompt, tool schemas, workspace, multi-turn history, and latest observation. Arrows lead to a bottom panel listing model dimensions, the per-token and per-trajectory KV footprint, and concurrency at 8,192 and 32,768 tokens on an eight-accelerator node."}
![](images/svg/prompt_context_window_anatomy.svg)
:::

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for .callout-notebook title="Sizing the attention state of an agent trajectory"}

**Problem**: A serving node has `{python} KvGeometry.n_acc_str` accelerators holding `{python} KvGeometry.node_hbm_str` of memory in total and serves the 70B grouped-query model just described. How many trajectories can it hold at once when each trajectory's context is `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_short_str`, `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str`, or `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_long_str` tokens?

**Math**:

Per token, $m_{\text{token}} =$ 2 $\times$ `{python} KvGeometry.n_layers_str` $\times$ `{python} KvGeometry.n_kv_heads_str` $\times$ `{python} KvGeometry.d_head_str` $\times$ 2 bytes $=$ `{python} KvGeometry.bytes_per_token_str` bytes, about `{python} KvGeometry.mb_per_token_str`.

Per trajectory, the footprint is `{python} KvGeometry.kv_short_str`, `{python} KvGeometry.kv_agent_str`, and `{python} KvGeometry.kv_long_str` at those three lengths.

The 16-bit weights take `{python} KvGeometry.weights_str`, and the runtime reserves `{python} KvGeometry.reserve_str` for activations and buffers, which leaves a KV pool of `{python} KvGeometry.node_hbm_str` $-$ `{python} KvGeometry.weights_str` $-$ `{python} KvGeometry.reserve_str` $=$ `{python} KvGeometry.kv_pool_str`.

Dividing the pool by each footprint gives `{python} KvGeometry.conc_short_str`, `{python} KvGeometry.conc_agent_str`, and `{python} KvGeometry.conc_long_str` concurrent trajectories.

**Systems insight**: The same node that holds `{python} KvGeometry.conc_short_str` short conversations holds only `{python} KvGeometry.conc_long_str` repository-scale trajectories. Context length, not arithmetic, sets how many agents a node can serve, so every token the harness keeps in context is a claim on a shared, fixed pool.

:::

Keeping each context near its effective working set (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}) keeps a trajectory near the left end of that range. Two other levers shrink the footprint without shortening the context. The first stores fewer bytes per token, either by model design, as grouped-query attention does (@sec-vol3-appendix-inference-kv-cache compares multi-head, multi-query, and grouped-query footprints), or by quantizing the stored keys and values to 8 bits, which halves $m_{\text{token}}$ at some risk to accuracy. The second discards the entries that receive little attention [@zhang2023h2o; @xiao2024streamingllm], which bounds the footprint but makes the state lossy, so a later step cannot recover what was dropped. The rest of this chapter takes the footprint as given and asks how the serving system holds it efficiently.

Three properties of agent trajectories make that hard. Their length is unknown in advance, because a task may finish in three turns or run for fifty. They fork, because test-time search (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute) samples several continuations from one shared prefix. They pause, because every tool call leaves the state idle for as long as the tool runs. In H·S·A terms (@sec-vol3-intro-hsa), this is where a long horizon becomes carried state that the accelerator must physically hold. Memory is a resource bound, and the invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}) places resource bounds in the runtime below the model, so the serving system and the harness, not the model, own every decision that follows. The first of the three properties, unknown length, is enough to break the simplest way of allocating this memory.

## Why Agent Workloads Strand Memory {#sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation}

A serving engine that admits a trajectory must decide how much memory to set aside for it, and the model cannot say in advance how long the trajectory will run. The simplest policy reserves one contiguous buffer sized for the longest context the deployment allows. That reservation never fails mid-trajectory, and it wastes most of what it reserves.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-static-reservation-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WORST-CASE RESERVATION EFFICIENCY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation prose; PagedWaste compares against it.
# │
# │ Goal: Show how little of a worst-case reservation an average trajectory uses.
# │ Show: 6.25 percent used, 93.75 percent idle; 48 reservations fill the pool.
# │ How: Scenario mean and cap (illustrative, not a measured trace); pool and
# │      bytes/token from KvGeometry.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class StaticReservation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    s_max = 32_768  # scenario: deployment context cap
    mean_tokens = 2_048  # scenario: mean trajectory length
    _bpt = KvGeometry.bytes_per_token
    _pool = KvGeometry.kv_pool

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    efficiency = mean_tokens / s_max
    reservations = int((_pool / (s_max * _bpt)).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(efficiency - 0.0625) < 1e-9, f"Expected 6.25 percent, got {efficiency}")
    check(reservations == 48, f"Expected 48 reservations, got {reservations}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    s_max_str = fmt_int(s_max)
    mean_tokens_str = fmt_int(mean_tokens)
    efficiency_pct_str = fmt_percent(efficiency, precision=2, style="prose")
    waste_pct_str = fmt_percent(1 - efficiency, precision=2, style="prose")
    reservations_str = fmt_int(reservations)
```

If trajectory lengths $S$ have mean $\mathbb{E}[S]$ and the engine reserves $S_{\max}$ tokens for each, the fraction of reserved memory that ever holds a token is $\eta_{\text{static}} = \mathbb{E}[S] / S_{\max}$. Suppose, for illustration, that the deployment caps contexts at `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str` tokens and the average trajectory ends at `{python} StaticReservation.mean_tokens_str`. Then only `{python} StaticReservation.efficiency_pct_str` of each reservation is ever written and `{python} StaticReservation.waste_pct_str` sits idle. The node from the previous section admits just `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` such reservations, the same number it could hold if every trajectory really did reach the cap.

This waste has two forms, shown in @fig-vol3-kv-fragmentation. Internal fragmentation is memory reserved for a trajectory but never written, either because the reservation assumed the worst case or because a buffer that grows by doubling leaves the second half empty. External fragmentation appears when trajectories of different sizes come and go. Free memory ends up scattered in gaps between live buffers, and a new trajectory that needs one contiguous region is refused even though the total free memory would hold it. Closing those gaps means stopping generation and copying live state to new addresses, which no latency target tolerates. Measurements of serving systems that allocate this way found that only 20 to 40 percent of KV memory held live tokens [@kwon2023vllm].

::: {#fig-vol3-kv-fragmentation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Two Ways Contiguous Reservation Wastes Memory**: Internal fragmentation (top) leaves reserved but unwritten slots inside a trajectory's buffer, from worst-case reservation or buffer doubling. External fragmentation (bottom) leaves free memory split across gaps, so request D, which needs one contiguous region as large as all the free memory combined, cannot be placed." fig-alt="Top panel shows two request buffers with hatched unused regions of 2,896 and 1,023 tokens. Bottom panel shows a 16 GB pool holding requests A, B, and C; after B departs, a 1 GB hole and a 5 GB tail remain, and request D needing 6 GB contiguous cannot be placed."}
![](images/svg/contiguous_memory_fragmentation.svg)
:::

Agent workloads make both forms worse. Their length distribution is wide. A task that succeeds on the first tool call ends within a few hundred tokens, while one that meets a failing build accumulates stack traces for dozens of turns. Short and long trajectories share the pool, so short ones punch holes between the long ones. Tool pauses add a third cost. A paused trajectory's buffer, including the part it has not yet written, stays reserved for as long as the tool runs, so memory is idle both inside the reservation and across time.

::: {#chk-05-memory-fragmentation .callout-checkpoint title="Memory stranding under worst-case reservation"}

The sizing estimate and the reservation arithmetic in this section are enough to answer these.

- [ ] **Reservation efficiency**: Why does reserving the context cap for every trajectory leave most reserved memory unwritten when lengths vary widely?
- [ ] **External fragmentation**: How can a contiguous allocator refuse a trajectory while the total free memory exceeds what it needs?
- [ ] **Tool pauses**: Why does a paused trajectory strand memory even if its reservation is exactly the right size?

:::

Every one of these costs comes from one assumption, that a trajectory's attention state must occupy one contiguous region sized in advance. Removing that assumption is the job of paging.

## Paged Blocks and Forks {#sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention}

A planning agent that samples four candidate plans from an 8,192-token context wants four continuations of the same prefix. Under contiguous allocation each candidate needs its own copy of that prefix, because each will append tokens after it. The engine copies gigabytes before the first candidate token is generated, and the copies crowd out other trajectories. The same mechanism that removes fragmentation also removes this copy.

**Paged KV allocation** stores attention state in fixed-size blocks, each holding the keys and values of $B$ tokens, drawn from a shared pool on demand [@kwon2023vllm]. The design borrows the page table from operating-system virtual memory, and here it does the same job. A per-trajectory block table maps the trajectory's logical block $l = \lfloor t/B \rfloor$ to whichever physical block holds it. The attention kernel reads the block table and gathers the blocks wherever they sit, so the trajectory's state no longer needs to be contiguous. The engine allocates a new block only when the last one fills, and when the trajectory ends its blocks return to a free list.

::: {#dfn-paged-kv-cache .callout-definition title="Paged KV cache"}

***Paged KV cache***\index{KV cache!paged}\index{Paged KV cache!definition} is a serving-memory layout that stores each trajectory's attention state in fixed-size blocks from a shared pool and maps the trajectory's token positions to those blocks through a per-trajectory block table.

1.  **Significance**: Memory is allocated as the trajectory grows rather than reserved for its worst case, so waste falls to the unfilled tail of each trajectory's last block and any free block can serve any trajectory.
2.  **Distinction**: A contiguous cache reserves one region per trajectory up front and must copy the whole prefix to fork; a paged cache allocates block by block and forks by copying block-table entries.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the block size as a free parameter. Small blocks enlarge block tables and add indirection to every attention step, while large blocks waste more tail space and share prefixes at a coarser grain.

:::

@Fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping shows the mapping with 16-token blocks. A 52-token sequence occupies four logical blocks. Its block table sends them to physical blocks 7, 2, 13, and 5, scattered across the pool, and only the last block has empty slots. Because every block is the same size, any free block can satisfy any request, and external fragmentation disappears.

::: {#fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Block Tables and Copy-on-Write Forks**: Left, a 52-token sequence split into 16-token logical blocks maps through its block table to scattered physical blocks, with only the tail block partly empty. Right, two branches forked from one parent share the parent's three full blocks by reference and allocate private blocks only for the tokens where they diverge." fig-alt="Left panel shows four logical blocks mapped by a per-sequence block table to physical blocks 7, 2, 13, and 5 in a pool of scattered frames. Right panel shows a parent sequence with shared prefix blocks 7, 2, and 13 at reference count 2, and two branches that alias those blocks and each own one private block, 18 and 24."}
![](images/svg/paged_attention_virtual_memory.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-paged-waste-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PAGED ALLOCATION WASTE VS. BLOCK SIZE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention prose.
# │
# │ Goal: Show that paged waste is a fraction of a percent and that paging
# │       multiplies the trajectories one pool admits.
# │ Show: 0.4 percent waste at 16-token blocks, 1.5 percent at 64; 780 vs. 48.
# │ How: calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens over the StaticReservation length model
# │      (capped exponential, a modeling assumption); pool from KvGeometry.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class PagedWaste:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    block_small, block_large = 16, 64
    _mean = StaticReservation.mean_tokens
    _s_max = StaticReservation.s_max
    _bpt = KvGeometry.bytes_per_token
    _pool = KvGeometry.kv_pool

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    alloc_small, frag_small = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(_mean, _s_max, block_small)
    alloc_large, frag_large = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(_mean, _s_max, block_large)
    conc_paged = int((_pool / (alloc_small * _bpt)).to("").magnitude)
    conc_ratio = conc_paged / StaticReservation.reservations

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(frag_small < 0.005, f"Expected under 0.5 percent waste at B=16, got {frag_small}")
    check(0.01 < frag_large < 0.02, f"Expected 1 to 2 percent waste at B=64, got {frag_large}")
    check(conc_paged == 780, f"Expected 780 paged trajectories, got {conc_paged}")
    check(15 < conc_ratio < 17, f"Prose claims about sixteen times as many, got {conc_ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    block_small_str = fmt_int(block_small)
    block_large_str = fmt_int(block_large)
    frag_small_pct_str = fmt_percent(frag_small, precision=1, style="prose")
    frag_large_pct_str = fmt_percent(frag_large, precision=1, style="prose")
    conc_paged_str = fmt_int(conc_paged)
```

Internal waste shrinks to the unfilled tail of each trajectory's last block, on average about $(B-1)/2$ tokens. For the same illustrative length distribution as before, `{python} PagedWaste.block_small_str`-token blocks waste `{python} PagedWaste.frag_small_pct_str` of allocated memory and `{python} PagedWaste.block_large_str`-token blocks waste `{python} PagedWaste.frag_large_pct_str`. The node that admitted `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` worst-case reservations now holds `{python} PagedWaste.conc_paged_str` trajectories of average length, about sixteen times as many. Smaller blocks would cut the tail further, but every block adds a block-table entry and an extra indirection when the kernel gathers keys and values, and the original paged design settled on 16-token blocks as the balance [@kwon2023vllm].

The block table also changes what a fork costs. Every physical block carries a reference count. Forking a trajectory copies the parent's block-table entries into the child and increments each shared block's count; no key or value is copied. The two sequences diverge lazily. When a branch first writes into a block whose count is greater than one, the engine gives that branch a private copy of the block and decrements the original's count, which is copy-on-write. The right half of @fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping shows two branches that share the parent's three full blocks and own one private block each. Pruning a branch, for example after a verifier rejects its candidate, decrements the counts of its blocks and frees only those that reach zero, so the shared prefix survives for the remaining siblings.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-fork-sharing-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COPY-ON-WRITE FORKS VS. CONTIGUOUS COPIES
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention prose (fork cost).
# │
# │ Goal: Price a best-of-four fork with and without prefix sharing, and show
# │       how many branches one pool admits either way.
# │ Show: 10.7 GB copied for four contiguous forks; 174 vs. 1,535 branches.
# │ How: calc_speculative_branch_capacity with KvGeometry pool and bytes/token;
# │      prefix and branch lengths are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple

class ForkSharing:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    prefix_tokens = 8_192  # scenario: shared planning context
    n_branches = 4  # scenario: best-of-four sampling
    branch_tokens = 1_024  # scenario: tokens per candidate
    block_tokens = PagedWaste.block_small
    _bpt = KvGeometry.bytes_per_token
    _pool = KvGeometry.kv_pool

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    copy_bytes = n_branches * prefix_tokens * _bpt
    cap_copy = calc_speculative_branch_capacity(_pool, prefix_tokens, branch_tokens, _bpt, cow=False)
    cap_cow = calc_speculative_branch_capacity(_pool, prefix_tokens, branch_tokens, _bpt, cow=True, page_block_tokens=block_tokens)
    cap_ratio = cap_cow / cap_copy

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(cap_copy == 174 and cap_cow == 1535, f"Expected 174/1535, got {cap_copy}/{cap_cow}")
    check(8 < cap_ratio < 9.5, f"Expected roughly ninefold, got {cap_ratio}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    prefix_tokens_str = fmt_int(prefix_tokens)
    branch_tokens_str = fmt_int(branch_tokens)
    copy_gb_str = fmt_memory(copy_bytes, unit=GB, precision=1)
    cap_copy_str = fmt_int(cap_copy)
    cap_cow_str = fmt_int(cap_cow)
    cap_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cap_ratio, precision=1)
```

For the planning agent that opened this section, four contiguous copies of the `{python} ForkSharing.prefix_tokens_str`-token prefix move `{python} ForkSharing.copy_gb_str` before any candidate runs. With copy-on-write the fork moves nothing. The capacity effect is larger still. If each candidate adds `{python} ForkSharing.branch_tokens_str` tokens, the node's pool holds `{python} ForkSharing.cap_copy_str` branches when each carries its own copy of the prefix and `{python} ForkSharing.cap_cow_str` when all of them share it, `{python} ForkSharing.cap_ratio_mult_str` as many. Best-of-$n$ sampling and self-consistency in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute depend on this sharing to be affordable, and group rollouts in reinforcement learning (@sec-vol3-rlvr), which sample many completions per prompt, are the largest shared-prefix fork workload an agent system runs.

A fork shares a prefix with its own parent. The next turn of the same agent, or a second agent started from the same system prompt, has no parent in the block table even though its first several thousand tokens are identical. Reusing state across those requests needs an index over prefixes, not a lineage.

## Prefix Caching Across Turns {#sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree}

Turn 21 of the coding agent re-sends everything turn 20 sent, plus the new test log. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost priced this re-sending and showed that reusing the shared prefix is the largest saving across a multi-turn trajectory. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging laid out the context so that the prefix stays byte-identical from turn to turn. This section describes the mechanism that turns that layout into saved prefill, and the harness decisions that make it succeed or fail.

### Matching a prefix

When a trajectory's request completes, the engine does not free its blocks immediately. It records them in an index keyed by token sequence, so that a later request beginning with the same tokens can attach to the same blocks and skip their prefill. A hash of the full prompt would recognize only exact repeats. The engine needs the longest cached prefix of each new request, so it indexes token sequences in a radix tree, a trie whose non-branching chains are compressed into single edges [@zheng2024sglang]. Each node binds a run of tokens to the physical blocks that hold their keys and values, a reference count of the running requests that use it, and the time it was last used.

::: {#dfn-radix-prefix-cache .callout-definition title="Radix prefix cache"}

***Radix prefix cache***\index{Prefix caching!radix tree}\index{Radix prefix cache!definition} is an index that maps token-sequence prefixes to the KV blocks computed for them, so that a new request reuses the blocks for its longest cached prefix and prefills only the remaining tokens.

1.  **Significance**: A hit on a shared prefix of $P$ tokens removes that prefix's prefill from the request, which for an agent re-sending its history every turn is most of the input.
2.  **Distinction**: A copy-on-write fork shares blocks along an explicit parent-child lineage, while a prefix cache shares blocks among unrelated requests that happen to begin with the same tokens.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming a near match counts. The cache reuses nothing past the first token that differs, so one volatile token early in the context forfeits every block after it.

:::

@Fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache shows such a tree. The system prompt sits at the root, pinned because three running requests use it. Branch A, a user goal with two active tool-call leaves, is also pinned. Branch B finished its turn and is no longer referenced, so its block waits on a least-recently-used (LRU) list. Only whole blocks are shared across requests. A request that matches 100 tokens with 16-token blocks reuses six full blocks and recomputes the last four tokens with its own suffix, because two requests appending different tokens into one shared partial block would corrupt each other's state.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_virtual_memory_margin_002.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Radix tree prefix matching diagram showing a 100-token shared system prefix partitioned into 6 full 16-token blocks with a 4-token unaligned tail truncated to prevent race conditions."}

*Only full blocks are shared across requests. A 100-token match reuses six 16-token blocks and recomputes the four-token tail.*
:::

::: {#fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Radix Prefix Cache with Leaf-First Eviction**: Left, a prefix tree whose nodes bind token ranges to physical KV blocks, with a pinned system-prompt root, an active branch with two tool-call leaves, and an idle branch. Right, the block residency table and the LRU list from which only unreferenced leaves are reclaimed under memory pressure." fig-alt="Left panel shows a radix tree with a root system-prompt node at reference count 3, branch A at reference count 2 with two leaf tool calls, and branch B at reference count 0 queued in an LRU list. Right panel shows a table mapping nodes to physical blocks, an LRU list feeding a free pool, and a row of physical blocks labeled by owner."}
![](images/svg/radix_prefix_tree_architecture.svg)
:::

Cached blocks compete with live trajectories for the same pool, so the engine evicts them under pressure. It evicts only unreferenced leaves, oldest first. A node cannot go before its children, because every descendant's state was computed from it. When a leaf is removed and its parent becomes an unreferenced leaf, the parent joins the eviction list in turn. The effect is that broadly shared prefixes, such as the system prompt and the tool definitions, stay resident longest, and one-off turns are reclaimed first.

### What breaks the hit rate

Attention state for a token depends on every token before it, so the cache can reuse state only up to the first token that differs (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}). Prefix caching is all or nothing from left to right. The engine cannot enforce a cache-friendly layout; it can only reward one, and the harness controls every input that decides the outcome. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging gives the layout rules. Seen from the cache, the common failures are these. Adding, removing, or reordering tool definitions mid-trajectory, for example when a tool server's list changes, alters the tokens near the head of the context and invalidates everything after them. A timestamp or request identifier placed in the system prompt makes every turn's prefix unique. Compaction that rewrites earlier history (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction) changes those tokens too, so the turn after compaction pays a full prefill, and a harness should compact rarely and in large steps rather than a little every turn. Non-canonical serialization, such as JSON keys emitted in a different order, produces different tokens for the same content.

The measure of all this is the prefix hit rate, the fraction of prompt tokens served from cache rather than prefilled:

$$H_{\text{prefix}} = \frac{\sum_{i} S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}}{\sum_{i} S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}}$$ {#eq-hprefix}

where request $i$ has prompt length $S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}$ and matched prefix $S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}$. A harness should log it per trajectory as it logs tokens and cost. A drop in hit rate after a harness change is usually the first sign that the change moved a volatile token toward the front of the context.

### Provider prompt caching

Most agent builders call a model through a hosted API rather than running the engine, and they meet the same mechanism as a billing feature. The provider caches the KV state of a prompt prefix and bills cached input tokens at a fraction of the normal input rate. Some interfaces reuse any sufficiently long matching prefix automatically. Others ask the caller to mark cache breakpoints, the positions up to which the prefix should be stored, and may charge extra for the tokens written into the cache. Cached entries expire after an idle time-to-live, typically minutes, because the provider runs the same leaf-first eviction as the radix cache, on a shared fleet.

Three harness consequences follow. The breakpoints belong at the boundaries of the stable zones in the layout of @sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging, after the tool definitions and after the long-lived history, so that each zone is cached once and reused. The time-to-live couples caching to tool waits. A tool that runs longer than the time-to-live returns to a cold cache, and the next turn pays full input price for the whole context, which is the provider-side version of the retain-or-evict decision in @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping. Finally, the hit rate becomes directly visible in the bill, as the ratio of cached to uncached input tokens the API reports, which makes it the cheapest metric of cache health a harness can track.

### Routing turns to the cache

A self-hosted deployment spreads trajectories across many serving replicas, and each replica has its own cache. If turn 21 lands on a different replica from turn 20, the cached prefix is on the wrong machine and the hit rate falls to zero. Cache-aware routing avoids this. The router hashes the prompt in block-sized chunks, looks up which replicas hold the longest matching prefix, and weighs that match against each replica's load, as @fig-vol3-cluster-prefix-routing shows. The simplest form is session affinity, which pins every turn of a trajectory to one replica. The load term matters, because pure affinity sends every trajectory that shares a popular system prompt to the same replica and builds a queue there.

::: {#fig-vol3-cluster-prefix-routing fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Cache-Aware Routing of Agent Turns**: The router hashes an incoming 40,000-token prompt in 16-token chunks, finds which replicas hold the longest matching prefix in a cluster-wide index, and scores each replica on cache match and queue load. The chosen replica holds 36,000 of the tokens and prefills only the 4,000-token turn delta." fig-alt="Three-stage diagram. Stage one hashes a 40,000-token prompt of system, tools, repository, and turn segments into chained 16-token chunk hashes. Stage two shows a cluster-wide prefix tree and a scoring formula weighing cache match against queue load. Stage three shows worker 1 selected with a 90 percent match, worker 2 penalized for 91 percent load, and cold workers 3 and 4."}
![](images/svg/cache_aware_prefix_routing.svg)
:::

Prefix caching removes the prefill of everything the trajectory has already sent. It cannot remove the prefill of what is new, and in an agent the new tokens arrive in large pieces, one tool observation at a time.

## Prefilling Observations {#sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill}

When the integration suite finishes, the harness appends its log to the context, perhaps twenty thousand tokens of test output. Before the model can emit the first token of its next step, the engine must prefill those tokens, and on a shared accelerator dozens of other trajectories are decoding at the same moment. The observation's prefill competes with their decoding.

The two phases stress different resources. Prefill processes many tokens per pass and is limited by arithmetic, while decode emits one token per trajectory per pass and is limited by how fast the weights stream from memory (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}); @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost states the per-call consequences and @sec-vol3-appendix-inference-roofline derives them. An engine that runs a large prefill as one pass stalls every co-scheduled decode for the length of that pass, so each of those trajectories sees a long pause between tokens. Chunked prefill splits the observation into fixed-size chunks and runs one chunk per pass alongside the ongoing decodes [@agrawal2024sarathi]. The resuming trajectory waits slightly longer for its first token, and every other trajectory keeps a bounded gap between tokens.

The observation's prefill is also where the harness and the cache meet. If the trajectory's earlier state is still resident, or reloaded, or found in the prefix cache, the engine prefills only the observation tokens. If that state was discarded during the tool wait, the engine prefills the entire context again, and a turn that should have cost twenty thousand tokens of prefill costs fifty thousand. Two harness decisions set this cost. The first is the observation's size. Trimming a log to the failing tests and their stack traces before staging it (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction) shortens this prefill directly. The second is what happened to the trajectory's state while the tool ran, which the next section takes up.

::: {#chk-05-paged-attention .callout-checkpoint title="Sharing and rebuilding attention state"}

These draw on paging, prefix caching, and observation prefill.

- [ ] **Copy-on-write forks**: Why does forking a trajectory into four candidates copy no keys or values, and when does a branch finally get private blocks?
- [ ] **Prefix hit rate**: A harness adds the current time to its system prompt. What happens to the hit rate, and why?
- [ ] **Provider caching**: Why can a tool that runs longer than the cache's time-to-live make the next turn cost the full input price?
- [ ] **Observation prefill**: What decides whether the turn after a tool call prefills only the observation or the whole context?

:::

## Retain, Evict, Recompute, or Offload {#sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping}

The coding agent's 32,768-token trajectory is paused on its forty-five-second test run. Its attention state could stay on the accelerator, be dropped and rebuilt from the tokens when the log returns, or be copied to host memory and brought back just before it is needed. Paging makes all three possible, because the state is a set of blocks the engine can free or move one at a time. Which one is right depends on how long the tool will run.

Holding the state has a cost that grows with the wait. A trajectory with $M_{\text{KV}}$ bytes of state paused for $T_{\text{wait}}$ seconds withholds

$$\mathcal{C}_{\text{hold}} = M_{\text{KV}} \cdot T_{\text{wait}}$$

byte-seconds of accelerator memory from every other trajectory, while computing nothing. This is the tool-wait memory tax. It is invisible in chat serving, where requests rarely pause, and it dominates agent serving, where most of a trajectory's wall-clock time is spent waiting on tools. The alternatives trade that tax for other costs, summarized in @tbl-vol3-reclamation-policies.

| **Policy**                 | **Where the state waits** | **Cost to resume**           | **Cost while waiting**                                      | **Fails when**                             |
|:---------------------------|:--------------------------|:-----------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------|
| **Retain**                 | Accelerator memory        | None                         | $M_{\text{KV}} \cdot T_{\text{wait}}$ of accelerator memory | Many long waits fill the pool              |
| **Evict and recompute**    | Nowhere                   | Prefill of the whole context | None                                                        | Contexts are long and resumes are frequent |
| **Offload to host memory** | Host memory               | Reload over the host link    | Host memory, transfer time                                  | Waits are shorter than the round trip      |
| **Park on flash storage**  | Local flash               | Slower reload                | Flash capacity                                              | Resume latency matters more than cost      |

: **Four Policies for a Paused Trajectory**: Where each policy keeps the attention state during a tool wait, what it costs to resume, what it costs while waiting, and the regime in which it fails. {#tbl-vol3-reclamation-policies tbl-colwidths="[18,17,22,23,20]"}

Because attention state is a function of its tokens (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}), dropping it loses no information, only work. The choice between the alternatives is therefore a cost comparison. Reloading $M_{\text{KV}} = S \cdot m_{\text{token}}$ bytes over a host link of bandwidth $B_{\text{link}}$ takes $T_{\text{reload}} = S \cdot m_{\text{token}} / B_{\text{link}}$. Recomputing it takes a prefill of $S$ tokens, about $2N$ operations per token for a model of $N$ parameters (@sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost), so $T_{\text{recompute}} \approx 2 N S / R_{\text{prefill}}$ at sustained prefill rate $R_{\text{prefill}}$. Both grow linearly with $S$, so their ratio,

$$\frac{T_{\text{reload}}}{T_{\text{recompute}}} = \frac{m_{\text{token}} \cdot R_{\text{prefill}}}{2 N \cdot B_{\text{link}}},$$

does not depend on context length at all. It is a property of the model and the machine, which means one comparison settles the question for every trajectory the deployment serves. Offloading also has a floor. The state must travel out and back before the tool returns, so offloading pays only when $T_{\text{wait}} > 2 T_{\text{reload}}$; for shorter waits the trajectory would stall on its own reload.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-tool-wait-break-even-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TOOL-WAIT BREAK-EVEN: RELOAD VS. RECOMPUTE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: notebook nbk-05-sizing-the-break-even-frontier-for;
# │          @fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff worked-example marker; the resident-state
# │          pitfall in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-fallacies; AgentCapacity (tool wait).
# │
# │ Goal: Compare reloading a 32,768-token trajectory's state over the host
# │       links with recomputing it, and price holding it through a 45 s wait.
# │ Show: 10.7 GB; 21 ms reload, 42 ms round trip; 1.3 s recompute; ~62x;
# │       ~15x at a quarter of link bandwidth; 483 GB-s held.
# │ How: Per-accelerator host-link bandwidth and peak FLOP/s from the H100 registry
# │      entry, eight links in parallel (TP=8 shards the KV state); 45 percent
# │      sustained prefill utilization and the 45 s wait are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_time, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_percent, MarkdownStr

class ToolWaitBreakEven:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    ctx_tokens = KvGeometry.ctx_agent
    tool_wait = 45 * second  # scenario: integration test run
    mfu = Literature.Training.MfuHigh * 0.9  # scenario: sustained prefill utilization (45 percent)
    _node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    _acc = _node.accelerator
    n_acc = _node.accelerators_per_node
    link_per_acc = _acc.interconnect.bandwidth
    peak_per_acc = _acc.compute.peak_flops
    n_params = Models.Language.Llama3_70B.parameters.to("count").magnitude
    m_kv = KvGeometry.kv_agent

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    link = n_acc * link_per_acc
    prefill_rate = n_acc * peak_per_acc * mfu
    t_reload = (m_kv / link).to(ms)
    t_round = 2 * t_reload
    recompute_flops = 2 * n_params * ctx_tokens * flop
    t_recompute = (recompute_flops / prefill_rate).to(second)
    ratio = (t_recompute / t_reload).to("").magnitude
    ratio_quarter = ratio / 4
    held = (m_kv * tool_wait).to(GB * second)
    wait_fraction = (t_round / tool_wait).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(20 < t_reload.magnitude < 22, f"Expected ~21 ms reload, got {t_reload}")
    check(1.2 < t_recompute.magnitude < 1.4, f"Expected ~1.3 s recompute, got {t_recompute}")
    check(55 < ratio < 70, f"Expected ~62x reload advantage, got {ratio}")
    check(ratio_quarter > 10, "Prose claims reload still wins by over 10x at quarter bandwidth")
    check(wait_fraction < 0.001, "Prose claims the round trip is under 0.1 percent of the wait")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    tool_wait_str = fmt_time(tool_wait, second, precision=0)
    ctx_tokens_str = fmt_int(ctx_tokens)
    n_params_b_str = fmt(n_params / 1e9, precision=1)
    mfu_pct_str = fmt_percent(mfu, precision=0, style="prose")
    link_per_acc_str = fmt_bandwidth(link_per_acc, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    link_str = fmt_bandwidth(link, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    prefill_rate_str = fmt_int(prefill_rate.to(TFLOPs / second).magnitude)
    m_kv_str = fmt_memory(m_kv, unit=GB, precision=1)
    t_reload_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_reload.magnitude)} ms")
    t_round_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_round.magnitude)} ms")
    recompute_pflop_str = fmt(recompute_flops.to(flop).magnitude / 1e15, precision=2)
    t_recompute_str = fmt_time(t_recompute, second, precision=1)
    ratio_mult_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(ratio)}×")
    ratio_quarter_mult_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(ratio_quarter)}×")
    held_str = fmt_int(held.magnitude)
```

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-the-break-even-frontier-for .callout-notebook title="Pricing a forty-five-second tool wait"}

**Problem**: The coding agent pauses at `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.ctx_tokens_str` tokens for a `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.tool_wait_str` test run on the eight-accelerator node from @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry. Should the engine keep its attention state, offload it to host memory, or drop it and recompute?

**Variables**:

* State to hold: $M_{\text{KV}} =$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.m_kv_str` (from the sizing estimate).
* Host links: each accelerator holds one-eighth of the state and has its own `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.link_per_acc_str` link, so the node moves state at up to $B_{\text{link}} =$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.link_str`.
* Prefill: `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.mfu_pct_str` of the node's peak rate, $R_{\text{prefill}} \approx$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.prefill_rate_str` TFLOP/s (an assumed sustained utilization).

**Math**:

Reload: `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.m_kv_str` / `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.link_str` $\approx$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.t_reload_str`, so the round trip out and back is `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.t_round_str`.

Recompute: $2 N S =$ 2 $\times$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.n_params_b_str` billion $\times$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.ctx_tokens_str` $\approx$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.recompute_pflop_str` $\times 10^{15}$ operations, which take `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.t_recompute_str` at the sustained rate.

Holding the state resident for the whole wait withholds `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.m_kv_str` $\times$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.tool_wait_str` $\approx$ `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.held_str` GB·s of accelerator memory.

**Result**: Reloading is about `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.ratio_mult_str` faster than recomputing, and the `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.t_round_str` round trip is well under a tenth of a percent of the wait. Even if the links sustain only a quarter of their rated bandwidth, reload still wins by about `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.ratio_quarter_mult_str`.

**Systems insight**: For any tool that runs longer than a few tens of milliseconds, offloading frees the accelerator memory for nearly the entire wait at almost no resume cost. Retention is right only for tools faster than the round trip, and recomputation is right only when host memory, not accelerator memory, is the scarce tier.

:::

@Fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff turns the comparison into a map. The boundary between retaining and offloading is the round trip, which grows with context length, so the retain region widens for long contexts but stays in the millisecond range. Almost every real tool call, a shell command, a build, a test run, a web fetch, falls in the offload region. At the far right are waits of minutes or hours, typically a person reviewing a proposed action. There the scarce resource becomes host memory itself, since thousands of paused sessions can each hold gigabytes. The engine can park that state on local flash, or simply drop it and recompute on resume, because a second or two of prefill is negligible next to a three-minute approval.

::: {#fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where a Paused Trajectory's State Should Wait**: Regimes by expected tool wait and context length. Waits shorter than the reload round trip favor retaining state on the accelerator; the boundary grows with context length. Most tool calls fall in the offload region. For waits of minutes or more, host memory becomes the scarce tier and the state is parked on flash or dropped and recomputed. The marker is the 32,768-token, 45-second example from the worked estimate." fig-alt="Log-log chart with expected tool wait from 1 ms to 1 hour on the x-axis and context length from 2,048 to 131,072 tokens on the y-axis. A green retain region lies left of a slanted round-trip line. A purple offload region extends to a dashed boundary at 1 minute. A gray park-or-drop region lies beyond it. An orange marker sits at 32,768 tokens and 45 seconds."}
![](images/svg/break_even_swapping_tradeoff.svg)
:::

Two refinements hide the reload entirely. The engine can prefetch, starting the reload shortly before the tool is expected to finish, so the state is back on the accelerator when the observation arrives. It can also overlap the reload with the observation's own prefill, streaming the earlier blocks back while the first observation chunk computes. Both depend on knowing roughly how long the tool will run, and that knowledge lives in the harness, not the engine. The harness knows whether a call is a file read, a test suite, or a human approval, and a tool's definition (@sec-vol3-tool-calling) can declare an expected duration alongside its other annotations. A harness that passes this hint to the serving layer lets it choose the right region in @fig-vol3-swapping-tradeoff; one that does not leaves the engine guessing from idle time alone.

The same decision appears at the API boundary in a different form. A hosted provider's cache time-to-live is its eviction policy, and the caller cannot offload. A harness that knows a tool will outlast the time-to-live can accept that the next turn will be uncached, or, where the interface allows, send a small request that refreshes the cache before it expires, trading a small charge for avoiding a full-price prefill. Recovering a trajectory after a crash, when all of its attention state is gone and must be rebuilt from its log, is the extreme case of evict and recompute, and @sec-vol3-durable-execution treats it.

A single paused trajectory now has a clear policy. A deployment runs hundreds of them at once, each alternating between generating and waiting, and the question for whoever provisions it is how much memory that mix needs.

## Capacity for Agent Workloads {#sec-vol3-kvcache-capacity-planning}

An operator sizing a node for a coding-agent service starts from the chat-serving habit of dividing memory by an average request. Agent trajectories break that estimate in three ways, each introduced earlier in the chapter. Their contexts grow with every turn, so the average at admission understates the average at the tenth turn. They fork, so one task briefly holds several branches. They pause, so memory stays occupied long after generation stops. Capacity planning has to account for all three, and for the prefix sharing that offsets them.

### Sizing the pool {#sec-vol3-kv-capacity-formulations}

Accelerator memory on a node divides among the weights, activation and runtime buffers, and the KV pool:

$$C_{\text{HBM}} = M_{\text{weights}} + M_{\text{activations}} + M_{\text{runtime}} + M_{\text{KV}}$$ {#eq-hbm-partition}

Only the last term of @eq-hbm-partition scales with the workload. For $n$ concurrent trajectories with average context $S_{\text{avg}}$ tokens and output $K_{\text{avg}}$ tokens, of which $S_{\text{shared}}$ tokens are a prefix common to all and held once, the pool must cover

$$M_{\text{KV}} \ge \left( S_{\text{shared}} + n \cdot \left( S_{\text{avg}} - S_{\text{shared}} + K_{\text{avg}} \right) \right) \cdot m_{\text{token}} + M_{\text{headroom}}$$ {#eq-kv-demand-shared}

where $M_{\text{headroom}}$ is free memory the allocator keeps so that a burst of decodes never finds the pool empty.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-agent-capacity-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AGENT CAPACITY WITH PREFIX SHARING AND TOOL-WAIT RESIDENCE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kv-capacity-formulations prose; the capacity pitfall in
# │          @sec-vol3-kv-cache-fallacies.
# │
# │ Goal: Show how prefix sharing and releasing state during tool waits each
# │       multiply the trajectories one node sustains.
# │ Show: 41 vs. 138 resident trajectories (3.4x); 0.82 vs. 8.2 turns/s (tenfold).
# │ How: @eq-kv-demand-shared with KvGeometry pool and bytes/token; Little's law
# │      with scenario generation time and the ToolWaitBreakEven tool wait.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class AgentCapacity:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    headroom = 0.10  # scenario: allocator headroom
    ctx_tokens = 32_768  # scenario: average accumulated context
    out_tokens = 2_048  # scenario: average output per trajectory
    shared_tokens = 24_576  # scenario: common prompt, tools, repo map
    t_generate = 5 * second  # scenario: decode time per turn
    t_wait = ToolWaitBreakEven.tool_wait
    _bpt = KvGeometry.bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    unique_tokens = ctx_tokens - shared_tokens
    usable = (1 - headroom) * KvGeometry.kv_pool
    per_unshared = (ctx_tokens + out_tokens) * _bpt
    b_unshared = int((usable / per_unshared).to("").magnitude)
    shared_bytes = shared_tokens * _bpt
    per_shared = (unique_tokens + out_tokens) * _bpt
    b_shared = int(((usable - shared_bytes) / per_shared).to("").magnitude)
    share_ratio = b_shared / b_unshared
    rate_retained = b_unshared / (t_generate + t_wait)
    rate_released = b_unshared / t_generate
    inflation = (rate_released / rate_retained).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(b_unshared == 41 and b_shared == 138, f"Expected 41/138, got {b_unshared}/{b_shared}")
    check(3.2 < share_ratio < 3.5, f"Expected ~3.4x from sharing, got {share_ratio}")
    check(abs(inflation - 10) < 1e-9, f"Prose claims tenfold, got {inflation}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    headroom_pct_str = fmt_percent(headroom, precision=0, style="prose")
    ctx_tokens_str = fmt_int(ctx_tokens)
    out_tokens_str = fmt_int(out_tokens)
    shared_tokens_str = fmt_int(shared_tokens)
    unique_tokens_str = fmt_int(unique_tokens)
    usable_str = fmt_memory(usable, unit=GB, precision=1)
    shared_gb_str = fmt_memory(shared_bytes, unit=GB, precision=1)
    b_unshared_str = fmt_int(b_unshared)
    b_shared_str = fmt_int(b_shared)
    share_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(share_ratio, precision=1)
    t_generate_str = fmt_time(t_generate, second, precision=0)
    rate_retained_str = fmt(rate_retained.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=2)
    rate_released_str = fmt(rate_released.to(1 / second).magnitude, precision=1)
```

Apply @eq-kv-demand-shared to the node from @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry with `{python} AgentCapacity.headroom_pct_str` headroom, which leaves `{python} AgentCapacity.usable_str` usable. If each trajectory carries `{python} AgentCapacity.ctx_tokens_str` tokens of context and produces `{python} AgentCapacity.out_tokens_str`, with nothing shared, the node holds `{python} AgentCapacity.b_unshared_str` trajectories. If `{python} AgentCapacity.shared_tokens_str` of those context tokens are a common system prompt, tool set, and repository map held once (`{python} AgentCapacity.shared_gb_str`), each trajectory's private state shrinks to `{python} AgentCapacity.unique_tokens_str` context tokens plus its output, and the same node holds `{python} AgentCapacity.b_shared_str`, `{python} AgentCapacity.share_ratio_mult_str` as many. The sharing is real only if the harness keeps that prefix byte-identical across trajectories, which is the layout discipline of @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree applied across a fleet rather than across turns.

Tool waits enter through Little's law [@little1961], which relates the average number of trajectories resident in a system to their arrival rate and residence time, $N_{\text{res}} = \lambda W$. For a fixed number of resident trajectories, the sustainable rate of turns is $\lambda = N_{\text{res}} / W$. Suppose each turn generates for `{python} AgentCapacity.t_generate_str` and then waits `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.tool_wait_str` on a tool. If attention state stays resident through the wait, a trajectory occupies memory for the whole fifty seconds, and the `{python} AgentCapacity.b_unshared_str` resident slots sustain `{python} AgentCapacity.rate_retained_str` turns per second. If state leaves the accelerator during the wait, as @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping recommends, each slot is occupied only while generating, and the same slots sustain `{python} AgentCapacity.rate_released_str` turns per second, tenfold more. For agent workloads the residence policy moves capacity more than any other single choice, and the cost moves to host memory, which is cheaper and larger. Rate limits, cost per accepted task, and the provisioning of whole fleets build on these per-node numbers in @sec-vol3-agent-economics.

### Watching occupancy {#sec-vol3-kv-telemetry-metrics}

Static sizing sets the pool; telemetry keeps the node out of trouble when the workload departs from the plan. The primary signal is KV utilization, the fraction of blocks allocated:

$$U_{\text{KV}} = \frac{N_{\text{allocated blocks}}}{N_{\text{total blocks}}}$$ {#eq-ukv}

Agent serving cannot hold the utilization of @eq-ukv near one. Every decode step may need a new block, a fork can claim many blocks at once, and a returning tool observation needs blocks for its whole prefill. When the pool runs dry the engine must preempt a running trajectory, offloading it synchronously or discarding its state, and the victim pays a reload or a full prefill in the middle of a turn. Median latency hardly moves as utilization climbs, because most steps still find a free block. Tail latency climbs steeply, as the schematic in @fig-vol3-latency-wall shows, and a harness waiting on the slowest step of a trajectory feels the tail, not the median.

::: {#fig-vol3-latency-wall fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Tail Latency Against KV Utilization (Schematic)**: Illustrative shape, not a measurement. Median time to first token and median gap between tokens stay flat as KV utilization rises, while tail latency climbs sharply once utilization passes an admission ceiling and the engine begins preempting and reloading trajectories." fig-alt="Semi-log chart of latency against KV cache utilization from 0 to 1. Median inter-token latency and median time to first token stay flat. Tail time to first token and tail inter-token latency rise steeply after an admission barrier marked at 0.88."}
![](images/svg/kv_utilization_latency_wall.svg)
:::

The response is admission control tied to these signals. The engine stops admitting new turns, and gates new forks within running trajectories, once utilization crosses a ceiling set below saturation, and it watches the prefix hit rate of @eq-hprefix alongside utilization. The two move together in a bad way. As the pool fills, the engine evicts cached prefixes first, the hit rate falls, the next turns pay full prefill, which holds blocks longer, and utilization climbs further. Queueing a new turn briefly is far cheaper than letting the node enter that loop, and a harness that sees rising queue time can shed or defer low-priority work before the loop starts.

These mechanisms are sound; the failures that reach production come from wrong beliefs about what attention state is and how agents use it.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-fallacies}

Most mistakes here come from carrying intuitions from chat serving or from databases into a structure that behaves like neither.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *The KV cache is the agent's memory.*

Because the cache holds something computed from every token the agent has seen, it is tempting to treat it as a memory tier between the context and a durable store, one that could be inspected for facts, patched when a fact changes, or relied on to carry a task across sessions. It can do none of these. The cached keys and values are intermediate activations, bound to their exact positions and meaningful only in aggregate inside attention. A block cannot be queried for what it says, edited to correct one fact, or moved into another context without changing the result. The cache also validates nothing. It preserves the state of whatever tokens were submitted, verified tool output and injected instructions alike. Attention state is a function of the exact token prefix (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}), so it holds nothing the tokens do not, including their errors, and it can be dropped and rebuilt from them at any time. Durable knowledge belongs in stores the runtime controls, which @sec-vol3-long-term-memory builds.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall:** *Keeping paused state resident regardless of wait time.*

Holding a trajectory's blocks through every tool call feels safe, because the resume is instant. For the 32,768-token trajectory of @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping, it means holding `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.m_kv_str` through a `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.tool_wait_str` test run, `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.held_str` GB·s of accelerator memory spent to avoid a `{python} ToolWaitBreakEven.t_round_str` round trip. Across a deployment, blanket retention divides the sustainable turn rate by the ratio of total turn time to generation time, tenfold in the capacity example. The engine should offload any trajectory whose expected wait exceeds the round trip, and the harness should tell it which waits those are.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy:** *A prefix-cache hit means the context is current.*

A prefix cache matches tokens, not the world they describe. If a system prompt says a file has a certain hash and the file then changes on disk, the next request that reuses the old text gets a perfect cache hit and a model conditioned on a stale description, served quickly and confidently. Only the file is authoritative, and every view derived from it, the staged text and the attention state computed from that text, goes stale when the file is written (principle \ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}). The defense is invalidation in the context (@sec-vol3-context-engineering-context-rot). The harness replaces or tombstones the stale observation before the next call, which changes tokens at that observation's position, so the cache still serves the stable prefix before it and recomputes from the edit onward. Putting a workspace digest at the head of the prompt would also prevent the stale hit, but it would place the most volatile token first and forfeit the cache for every turn after every write.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall:** *Planning capacity from average isolated requests.*

Dividing the KV pool by the average request footprint gives a number that holds for chat and fails for agents. Correlated branching lets one task claim many blocks within a few decode steps, so demand arrives in bursts that average-based headroom does not absorb. Tool waits stretch residence time, and by Little's law the resident population at a given arrival rate grows in proportion (@sec-vol3-kv-capacity-formulations). Contexts grow across turns, so an average taken at admission understates the average at turn ten. A pool sized this way runs near saturation, where preemptions evict cached prefixes, prefix hit rate collapses, full prefills hold blocks longer, and tail latency climbs. Capacity has to be planned against peak branching and the actual wait-time distribution, with admission control set well below saturation.
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-kv-cache-summary}

Every token an agent keeps in context occupies accelerator memory as attention state, at a per-token cost fixed by model geometry. For a long trajectory that state, not the weights, decides how many agents a node can serve. Agent trajectories make it hard to hold efficiently because their length is unknown, they fork, and they pause on tools. Paged blocks remove the waste of worst-case reservation and let forks share a prefix by reference. A radix prefix cache extends that sharing across turns and across trajectories, rewarding a harness that keeps its prefix stable and punishing one that does not. When a tool call pauses a trajectory, the choice among retaining, offloading, and recomputing is a cost comparison whose answer, for almost every real tool, is to move the state off the accelerator and bring it back before the tool returns.

The recurring theme is that the engine holds the state while the harness shapes it. Context length, prefix stability, compaction timing, observation size, and expected tool duration are all harness decisions, and each one moves memory, prefill work, and capacity by a large factor.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Attention state is a shared, disposable resource that the harness shapes"}

* **Context length sets agent capacity**: A trajectory's KV footprint is its token count times a per-token cost fixed by model geometry, so the same node that serves `{python} KvGeometry.conc_short_str` short contexts serves only `{python} KvGeometry.conc_long_str` repository-scale ones.
* **Paging turns reservations into usage**: Fixed-size blocks allocated on demand cut waste from most of each reservation to a fraction of a percent, and copy-on-write lets best-of-$n$ branches share one prefix instead of copying it.
* **Prefix reuse is all or nothing from the left**: The cache reuses state only up to the first differing token, so tool-list changes, early timestamps, and frequent compaction each forfeit the largest saving an agent has across turns.
* **Offload paused state for real tool waits**: Reloading state is tens of times faster than recomputing it, and the ratio does not depend on context length, so any tool slower than the reload round trip should free accelerator memory while it runs.
* **Residence policy dominates agent capacity**: By Little's law, keeping state resident through tool waits divides the sustainable turn rate by total turn time over generation time, tenfold in this chapter's example.

:::

Paging, prefix sharing, and offload all rest on one property of attention state (principle \ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}). It is a function of the exact token prefix, so it can be shared only across identical prefixes and rebuilt from the tokens at any time. That property is why eviction costs recomputation and never task knowledge, and why the reload-to-recompute ratio does not depend on context length, which let the chapter reduce the pause decision to one round-trip threshold. It is also why the harness can reason in turns, tool calls, and trajectories while the serving engine treats their attention state as blocks to page, share, move, or drop on cost.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From serving state to durable memory"}

What must outlive the session, and how does it come back without poisoning the context?

Attention state is derived and disposable. It lives on one serving node, disappears when a trajectory is evicted or a process restarts, and can always be rebuilt from its tokens. The records those tokens came from are different. A repository, a database, a user's preferences, and the lessons an agent has learned must persist across sessions and return only when they are relevant, current, and authorized. @Sec-vol3-long-term-memory turns to that durable state, covering what an agent should store, how it retrieves evidence into the next context, and how it writes back to memory without corrupting what it will read later.

:::
